tagline: Deserts, oil, and Islam's holiest cities
overview:
Saudi Arabia fills most of the Arabian Peninsula, the large wedge of land between Africa and Asia, with the Red Sea on one side and the Persian Gulf on the other. At about 2.15 million km² it is the largest country in the Middle East, roughly a quarter the size of the United States, and most of it is desert.

About 36 million people live in Saudi Arabia, including millions of foreign workers. Arabic is the official language. Riyadh, the capital, is a modern city in the center of the country, while Jeddah is the Red Sea port and Mecca and Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam, lie inland from it.

Saudi Arabia is a monarchy ruled by the Al Saud family. It holds some of the world's largest oil reserves, and the government has been investing oil money in new cities, tourism, entertainment and sport as it tries to build an economy less dependent on petroleum.
landAndNature: The Rub al Khali, the Empty Quarter, covers the south: about 650,000 km² of sand, the largest continuous sand desert on the planet, with dunes up to 250 meters tall. The Nafud desert in the north has red-tinted sand. Mountains run down the western edge along the Red Sea, rising above 3,000 meters near the Yemeni border, where the Asir highlands catch enough monsoon rain for terraced farms, juniper forests and even fog. Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers at all; water comes from underground aquifers and desalination plants. Arabian oryx, sand cats, hyenas and the Arabian leopard, now extremely rare, survive in the wild, while the Red Sea's reefs are among the healthiest and least damaged anywhere.
peopleAndCulture: Islam shapes daily life: prayers five times a day, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and the feasts of Eid. Every year millions of Muslims from around the world travel to Mecca for the hajj pilgrimage, walking seven times around the Kaaba, a duty for every Muslim who is able. Kabsa, spiced rice with lamb or chicken, is served on large shared platters, and Arabic coffee with dates greets guests. Men often wear a white thobe and a checked headscarf; women commonly wear an abaya. Camel racing, falconry and the ardah sword dance are old traditions, while soccer fills stadiums and Saudi clubs have signed some of the world's most famous players.
history: Trading caravans carrying frankincense and spices crossed Arabia thousands of years ago, and the Nabataeans carved tombs into cliffs at Hegra, now the country's first World Heritage site. The Prophet Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 and the religion of Islam began here, spreading across three continents within a century. For centuries the region was divided among tribes and ruled in part from Ottoman Istanbul. In the 1700s the Al Saud family allied with the religious reformer Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and after long campaigns Abdulaziz ibn Saud united most of the peninsula, founding the modern kingdom in 1932. Oil was discovered in 1938, transforming a poor desert country into a wealthy one within a generation. Since 2017 the kingdom has lifted rules such as its ban on women driving.
funFacts: Saudi Arabia has no permanent rivers or lakes, and is one of the world's largest producers of desalinated seawater.
The Empty Quarter is so vast that some of its dunes have never been crossed on foot or by vehicle.
Mecca's Grand Mosque can hold more than a million worshippers at once during the hajj pilgrimage.
Al-Ahsa in the east is one of the largest oasis systems in the world, with more than two million date palms.
Saudi Arabia uses the Islamic lunar calendar for religious life, so Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each year.
